script.stored_text_completeness: All 19266 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored ending is complete ("See you in the next video."); one dropped word ("things you do make you than things you own", presumably "happier"); the Carter/Colton frame is a composite story, and its "$800,000 in foregone wealth" reuses the separate $400/month calculation; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: I want to tell you about two brothers, Carter and Colton. Same parents, same house, same Cincinnati suburb, same underfunded public school. Their dad drove a city bus for 32 years. When they both graduated and started working, they each took home roughly $3,200 a month after taxes. Fast forward to today, Carter is 46. He books last minute flights on a Tuesday because he felt like seeing a friend in Austin. He doesn't check his account first, he just
script.ending_words: money arrives in an ordinary week that nobody around you will ever notice, but you will in 20 years on a Tuesday when you book a flight without checking your account first. If this one hit different, subscribe. We cover this every week. Drop a comment below. Which generation do you think got hit hardest by this trap and why? I'll be reading everyone. See you in the next video.
script.analysis: Full 19266 canonical characters read. A single-narrator explainer framed by two composite brothers (Carter and Colton): hook, Goldman paycheck-to-paycheck statistic, definition of lifestyle inflation, a generational history (boomers, Gen X credit, millennials, Gen Z BNPL and social media), four psychological mechanisms (hedonic adaptation, social comparison, Diderot effect, present bias), compounding examples ($400 start-age, rent upgrade, subscriptions, raises), Millionaire Next Door and Buffett, experiences vs things, systems (Save More Tomorrow, friction, conscious spending, audits), and a callback close. Arithmetic reproduces; the 1980 credit figure is overstated and several survey numbers are unsourced.
beat_map: Hook: Carter and Colton, same start, different outcomes.
Gen X: credit cards and HELOCs.
Millennials: two-income trap and the experience economy.
Gen Z: BNPL and social comparison.
Four mechanisms: hedonic adaptation, social comparison, Diderot, present bias.
Compounding: start age, rent, subscriptions, raises.
Experiences vs things; income and happiness.
Systems: Save More Tomorrow, friction, conscious spending, audit.
